title: Community thermal composition in 75 monitoring networks followed about 12% of its own spatial temperature gradient in time; a lag fit gives fast adjustment to a small target (1948-2025)
abstract: Question: which fraction of its own spatial community temperature index (CTI) gradient does a monitoring network follow in time, and is the deficit a lag? Data: 73 BioTIME 2.0 studies plus the North American Breeding Bird Survey (1966-2025) and the UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (1973-2024): 75 networks, 8,529 grid-box sites, 183,626 site-years, 1948-2025; GHCN_CAMS air temperature and HadISST or OISST sea surface temperature. Method: cross-fitted species temperature indices inside each network; spatial slope b_space of site CTI on site climatology; within-site slopes on temperature anomalies (fast) and site warming trends (slow); random-effects synthesis; species-shuffle nulls; a lag-model emulator on each network's own temperature record. Results: the pooled fast fraction was 0.020 (95% CI 0.005-0.039) and the pooled slow fraction 0.12 (0.02-0.28) of b_space; across seven variants the slow fraction was at most 0.19. A pure lag calibrated by the fast response predicted a median slow fraction of 0.54; the observed median was 0.15 (65% of networks below, p = 0.013). A two-parameter partial-adjustment fit gave an adjustment rate of 0.26 per year (0.17-0.41; half-life 2.3 years) and an equilibrium fraction of 0.28 (0.12-0.54); a pure lag with full spatial equivalence fitted worse. Terrestrial networks had a slow fraction of 0.18 (0.04-0.35) and freshwater networks -0.06 (-0.20-0.05). The marine value (0.37 with HadISST) was not robust to OISST (-0.07). Endotherms and ectotherms did not differ robustly. Species-shuffle nulls were exceeded in combination (Stouffer z 2.5-2.7) but in only 3-4 single networks. Conclusion: weak climate tracking is general and is mainly a small temporal sensitivity relative to spatial gradients, not a long lag. Limitations: temperature proxies for benthic and freshwater habitats, network-internal STIs that include non-thermal gradients, heterogeneous BioTIME methods, and a single-rate lag model.
